meta.ogDescription: Not Yogi Berra. The earliest citation is Royals outfielder Jim Wohlford, April 1974. Berra's name isn't attached until January 1979.

answer.label: Not Yogi Berra — actually Jim Wohlford
answer.sourceLine: The earliest citation in Barry Popik’s dated chronology is a 4 April 1974 column in the Maryville (MO) Daily Forum, which quotes Kansas City Royals outfielder Jim Wohlford: “Ninety per cent of this game is half mental.” Yogi Berra is not credited with the line in print until 28 January 1979, almost five years later, and Wikiquote files it under Disputed.

source.heading: The 1974 column that got there first

docMeta.dd: Jim Wohlford, Kansas City Royals outfielder
“‘Needlee’ Wohlford May Have Last Laugh” by Steve Cameron
Maryville (MO) Daily Forum, 4 April 1974, p. 9, cols. 1–2
28 January 1979 — Dick Young’s column, Aberdeen (SD) American News, p. 11

source.excerpt: He’s the kind of guy who manages, quite innocently, to always say the kind of thing that will haunt him (‘Ninety per cent of this game is half mental…’).
trail: 4 April 1974 — the earliest citation in Barry Popik’s chronology ↗. Steve Cameron’s column in the Maryville (MO) Daily Forum quotes Royals outfielder Jim Wohlford: “Ninety per cent of this game is half mental.”
April 1977 — the same sentence is credited to Phillies manager Danny Ozark ↗ in the Des Moines Register (19 April) and the St. Petersburg Times (26 April), three years after Wohlford.
28 January 1979 — the first citation crediting Yogi Berra ↗, in Dick Young’s syndicated column in the Aberdeen (SD) American News — the sentence, then a dash, then Berra’s name.
Today — Wikiquote files the line under Disputed ↗, naming Wohlford as the first to say it, while quote sites keep printing the smoothed-out version under Berra’s name.
source.excerptNote: The 1974 printing spells it “per cent” as two words. Note also how the columnist frames it — parenthetically, as an example of the sort of thing Wohlford is already known for saying, rather than as a fresh remark being reported for the first time.

source.rightsHolder: Steve Cameron and the Maryville (MO) Daily Forum for the 1974 column; Jim Wohlford as the speaker quoted
source.rightsNote: Nothing here is public domain: the earliest documented printing is a newspaper column of 4 April 1974, more than four decades after the pre-1931 cutoff that governs US public domain, and the Berra-branded rewrites were printed later still. We make no claim about whether a seven-word spoken quip is itself protectable expression — only that no pre-1931 source for it exists.

author.name: Jim Wohlford
author.kicker: The man who actually said it
author.heading: The reserve outfielder behind the most-quoted line he never got credit for
author.metaLine: born 1951 · Major-league outfielder, 1972–1986 · Royals, Brewers, Giants, Expos
author.bio: James Eugene Wohlford was born 28 February 1951 in Visalia, California, and debuted for the Kansas City Royals on 1 September 1972. Over fifteen seasons with the Royals, Milwaukee Brewers, San Francisco Giants and Montreal Expos he played 1,220 games and batted .260, mostly as a reserve and defensive-replacement outfielder. He never made an All-Star team — and yet his Wikipedia entry leads on the fact that he “became notable” for a single sentence that the rest of the world has spent fifty years crediting to somebody else.

misattribution.heading: Three men, one sentence
misattribution.intro: This is a line with a queue of claimants, and the famous one joined the queue last. Here is who has been credited, and when the paper trail says each credit begins.

items.why: The first citation crediting Berra that Popik documents ↗ is 28 January 1979 — Dick Young’s syndicated column in the Aberdeen (SD) American News, which prints the sentence and simply appends Berra’s name. That is almost five years after the line is already in print as Wohlford’s. Wikiquote lists it under Disputed ↗, not among his sourced Yogiisms.

The Phillies manager (1923–2009) picked the line up in the middle. Popik’s chronology ↗ credits it to Ozark in the Des Moines Register of 19 April 1977 and the St. Petersburg Times of 26 April 1977 — three years after Wohlford, two before Berra. Ozark was routinely lampooned for malapropisms ↗, which made him a natural magnet too.

items.who: “Baseball is ninety percent mental, and the other half is physical”
items.why: This smoother version is what quote sites, mugs and posters actually print under Berra’s name. Popik treats it as a popular variation of the line ↗, not as the wording that was first recorded. The 1974 printing reads “Ninety per cent of this game is half mental” — “per cent” as two words, “this game” rather than “baseball,” and no second clause at all.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence that got into print first was Jim Wohlford’s, in April 1974 — and Popik’s dated chronology ↗ contains nothing earlier. Berra usually receives the credit; Wohlford said it first.

context.heading: Why the line ended up in Berra’s mouth
lead: Wohlford’s sentence is a perfect specimen of a particular kind of joke — a percentage that does not add up, delivered flat. That shape had a famous owner long before 1974. By the mid-1970s Yogi Berra was already the recognised brand for cheerfully self-contradicting arithmetic, so any orphaned line with that shape drifted toward him the way loose iron drifts toward a magnet.

The paper trail shows the drift happening. In April 1974 it is a young Royals outfielder’s catchphrase. By April 1977 sportswriters are pinning it on Phillies manager Danny Ozark, another man collected for his malapropisms. By January 1979 a syndicated New York columnist prints it with Berra’s name attached and no explanation — and that is the version that stuck, because it was the one that sounded most like itself.
context.detailsSummary: But didn’t Berra claim it himself?
detailsBody: Complicating things: CBS Sports, citing The New York Times, reports that Berra took credit for this one in his own book ↗ — unlike “déjà vu all over again,” which he initially denied. That is worth stating plainly rather than hiding.

It does not move the earliest attestation. Berra’s claim came decades after Wohlford was quoted saying it in 1974, and a later claim by a famous man does not outrank a contemporaneous newspaper citation of an obscure one. Berra may well have said a version of it — a line this catchy gets repeated by everyone in a dugout — but saying it is not the same as coining it.
Berra himself supplied the caveat that ought to govern every page like this one. Wikiquote records, among his genuinely sourced Yogiisms, his admission that he really didn’t say everything he said.
context.pull: I really didn’t say everything I said.
